prompt: Order the steps to get a white-label app into the stores.

items.label: Client opens its store accounts and invites Oyelabs
Rebranded builds pass QA and UAT sign-off
Listing assets, privacy policy URL and review notes ready
Apps approved by Apple and Google
Release the apps and smoke-test production

task.explanation: Accounts, rebranded builds and UAT, store listing, submission, approval, then go-live.

prompt: Order these stages of a white-label project.

task.explanation: Demo, gap analysis, (brand kit and accounts), configuration, builds and UAT, (listing), submission, go-live.

prompt: White-label fitness app for a reseller's gym client. Builds passed QA. The gym has no Apple Developer account. The reseller: "Publish under your account, we'll move it later."

task.prompt: Choose the best option at each step.

steps.question: What do you reply?
options: Agree, to hit the date
Decline: the gym's own account submits; ours risks 4.2.6
Use the reseller's account instead
steps.explanation: Apps are submitted only from the client's own accounts; Guideline 4.2.6 rejects template apps not submitted by the content provider.

steps.question: What must the gym do?
options: Enrol as an organisation and invite Oyelabs
Enrol in the owner's personal name
Send us its Apple ID password
steps.explanation: Businesses enrol as an organisation (legal entity, D-U-N-S) and invite the agency with a role.

steps.question: How do you report it?
options: Client dependency logged; schedule amber
Keep it green until the date slips
Red, and stop all work
steps.explanation: At risk but recoverable with action is amber; log the client dependency in writing.

prompt: A white-label onboarding checklist. Mark the lines that break account ownership or security.

segments.text: Logo as SVG or 1024×1024 PNG with transparency – client.
Apple Developer account: use the Oyelabs account for now.
segments.issue: Store accounts must be in the client's name.

segments.text: Google Play Console in the client's name, Oyelabs invited with release permissions.
Hosting and domain registered by our freelancer, in his name.
segments.issue: Accounts opened in a freelancer's name are a known pitfall.

segments.text: Payment gateway live keys: client sends them over WhatsApp.
segments.issue: Keys go only through an approved secure channel.

segments.text: Privacy policy and terms published on the client's domain – client.
SMS provider with a registered sender ID – client.

prompt: Two store reviews come back for a white-label app. Typically, who carries each fix?

task.prompt: Choose the best option at each step.

steps.question: Apple: the app crashes on launch on the reviewer's device.
options: Our build problem: typically fixed free
Billable to the client
The client's job to fix
steps.explanation: Rejections caused by the build or the agency's work are typically fixed free.

steps.question: Google: the privacy policy URL on the client's domain returns 404.
options: Free: we fix the client's site
Client's responsibility, or billable
Resubmit unchanged
steps.explanation: Rejections caused by client content or legal pages are typically billable or the client's responsibility.

prompt: Apple requires a newer SDK, so every white-label instance needs core 4.3. Three instances are uncustomised; one has a forked checkout.

task.prompt: Choose the best option at each step.

steps.question: When do you assess the forked instance's effort?
options: Before the upgrade; quote it as a CR or support work
During the upgrade, as conflicts appear
After release, if anything broke
steps.explanation: Customisation impact is assessed before the upgrade and quoted; discovering it mid-upgrade is a known pitfall.

steps.question: Typically, what covers the uncustomised upgrades?
options: The licence or support plan
A CR per instance
A new SOW
steps.explanation: A core upgrade of an uncustomised instance is typically covered by the licence or support plan.

prompt: A sales draft of a gap analysis. Mark the lines that misclassify work or will hurt upgrades.

segments.text: Logo, colours and font via the theme file: configuration, in setup.
New substitution-approval step: configuration, included in setup.
segments.issue: It needs code: customisation, estimated and quoted before setup.

segments.text: Delivery zones and fees set in the admin panel: configuration.
Loyalty points: built by editing the core checkout files.
segments.issue: Customisation belongs in a separate custom module, not core files.

segments.text: Table reservations: existing add-on, switched on by a feature toggle.
All customisations estimated and approved in writing before setup.

prompt: In a white-label setup, which of these is configuration?

options: Setting the currency and service areas in the admin panel
Adding a checkout step the product doesn't support
Building a new reporting module
Editing the core checkout code
mcq.explanation: Configuration uses options the product already supports (settings, panels, toggles, themes) without new code; anything needing code is customisation.

prompt: Apple rejects a white-label app under Guideline 4.2.6. What does this usually mean?

options: A template app not submitted by the content provider's own account
The privacy policy URL is missing
The app crashed during review
The screenshots don't match the app
mcq.explanation: 4.2.6 covers apps created from a commercialised template, unless submitted by the provider of the app's content. Submitting from the client's own account avoids it.

prompt: Why should the store accounts be in the end client's name?

options: The client stays in control; later transfers are slow
Agencies cannot pay the store fees
Stores forbid invited team members
It makes builds compile faster
mcq.explanation: Client-owned accounts keep the client in control, avoid slow transfers later, and match store rules that expect the brand owner as seller.

prompt: Why build a client's customisation as a separate custom module instead of editing core files?

options: So core upgrades need only a compatibility check
Because modules are always free to build
So the client can edit the core itself
Because stores reject edited core files
mcq.explanation: A separate module keeps the core upgradable; edits to core files create merge conflicts and costly upgrades.
